cards.title: February Revolution in Russia
cards.it: 1917 was a tumultuous year in Russia, with successive revolutions overthrowing governments. Events #1 to #3 represent a number of effects Russian disintegration had in Finland. On one hand, the so-called activists—who for years had been secretly channeling Finnish men to Germany to receive military training (the so-called jaegers)—got new...

cards.it: See above.

cards.title: October Revolution in Russia
cards.it: See above.

cards.title: Strikes
cards.it: On several occasions throughout 1917, the working-class movement used strikes as a means for advancing their political aims. In the absence of an effective national police force, often these strikes would turn violent and lead to deaths (see #20 The Leg of Tokoi’s Chair).

cards.title: "Powers Act"
cards.it: This act of the Finnish parliament was prepared during the latter half of 1917. On one hand, it meant independence and a transfer of power from Russia to the Finnish Parliament. It was thus welcomed across the Finnish political spectrum. On the other hand, the act would transfer power to the parliament and thus reflect its then current...

cards.title: General Election
cards.it: The general election of October 1917 in Finland was held in an antagonistic atmosphere of riots, unrest, and strikes. In that election, the Social Democratic Party received more votes than in the previous election—but lost their absolute majority in the parliament—as the conservative and centrist parties put their differences aside to form a...

cards.title: "We Demand" Manifesto
cards.it: Published in November 1917 by the Social Democratic Party, the manifesto contained demands for a number of reforms, among others, the introduction of an eight-hour work day. The key demands of the manifesto—including the eight-hour work day—were eventually ratified after a general strike (Event #8).

cards.title: Weapons and Jaeger from Germany?
cards.it: Jaeger were Finnish volunteers who, since 1914, had been receiving military training in Germany. The return of the jaeger, starting in October 1917, greatly strengthened the Senate forces, affording them much-needed trained and disciplined soldiers and leaders. The historian Alapuro (1988: 157-158) wrote: A group of ‘Activists’ had worked for...

cards.title: Weapons from Lenin?
cards.it: After coming to power in November 1917, Lenin and the Bolsheviks in Russia were attempting to supply the Red rebels in Finland with weaponry (see Event #14 below). Despite this assistance, the aims of the Finnish Reds and the Russian Bolsheviks did not entirely coincide. The historian Seppo Hentilä wrote (Jussila et al 1999: 118): In late...

cards.title: Food Supply Issues
cards.it: The historian Risto Alapuro (1988: 163) wrote: The worsening food shortage played a central role in radicalizing the masses. In late September [1917] party leaders stated that the masses were growing restless over the food situation, and a few days before the foundation of the national security guard organization, party and trade union leaders...

cards.title: Joblessness
cards.it: As a part of the Russian Empire, Finland’s economy depended heavily on Russia’s. Initially, Russian participation in the First World War stimulated agricultural production, as well as manufacturing in Finland. Eventually, however, and especially from the Summer of 1917 on, instability in Russia led to decreased demand, then to further economic...

cards.title: Cannons
cards.it: Alongside Armored Trains (see Event #15 Trains below), cannons were some of the heavier weaponry used in the Finnish Civil War. These were acquired from Russian garrisons in Finland, or secretly from the Germans (Event #10) and from the Bolsheviks in Russia. For example, on 27 January, 1918, on Lenin’s orders, a weapons train carrying 10,000...

cards.title: Trains
cards.it: In 1918, in Finland, the railways represented virtually the only viable mode of speedy mass transportation. Through the long Winter and late into the Spring, snow and ice would hinder road-based transportation in a country whose motorized transportation and road networks were underdeveloped anyway. cards.title: Jaeger
cards.it: See Event #10 above. The shaded Event-text refers to the historical role of the few Russian military advisers that worked on the Reds’ side. One of them was Colonel Mihail Svetsnikov (1882-1938), the former chief of staff of the Russian 106th Army Division. He advised the Reds, among others, in the battle of Tampere (Event #40).

cards.title: Trains
cards.it: See #15 above. A Finnish family peels tree bark for making bark bread.

cards.title: Mobilization in the Periphery
cards.it: All Bridges Burning focuses on the events in central and southern Finland, where most of the civil war was fought (and most of the populace lived). In the early parts of the war, some fighting also took place in the northern parts of the country. For example, the town of Oulu (just beyond the map’s northern edge) and its surroundings were said...

cards.title: Political Struggle
cards.it: Throughout 1917 and the build-up to the Finnish Civil War, a parliamentary struggle for political reforms went on. Strikes, the mobilization of the guards, and an effective power vacuum on the streets, gave rise to many opportunities for political blackmail.

cards.title: The Leg of Tokoi's Chair
cards.it: The “leg of Tokoi’s chair” was the nickname given to the batons carried by the replacement police force (essentially, militias) that in the course of 1917, in a situation of deteriorating law and order throughout the country, was ordered by the Finnish Senate to replace the forces of the Russian gendarmerie in Finland. Oskari Tokoi (1873-1963),...

cards.title: Workers' Halls
cards.it: Workers’ Halls, built throughout the country, served as central meeting points for the Reds, offering premises for political organization and activity.

cards.title: Propaganda — 1st
cards.it: Pictured on the card is a political drawing from Velikulta magazine, published in 1917. The drawing argues that despite svaboda—liberation—achieved by the workers in Russia, working-class demonstrations in Finland were continuing to be suppressed by the bourgeoisie, represented by the man in the white coat, as well as the men wearing a white...

cards.title: Propaganda — 2nd
cards.it: This card features a White Senate propaganda poster. It attempts to illustrate that a far larger portion of Finland was in White, rather than in Red, hands. What the poster fails to mention is that by far the largest portion of the Finnish population lived in the southern areas, which was controlled by the Reds. position as the workers movement...

cards.title: Red Revolt!
cards.it: (Pivotal Event) On 27 January, 1918, the Reds launched a revolt, taking control of the major population centers in the south of the country. The historian Alapuro (1988: 172-173) wrote: Even the party leadership could not ignore the government’s intention to put down the worker security guards as soon as it felt strong enough. After encounters...

cards.title: Disarming Russian Garrisons
cards.it: Russian garrisons existed all over Finland in 1917. As political instability in Russia grew, many garrisons gradually evaporated into thin air as soldiers were either ordered to head home or did so on their own initiative. One attempt to disarm a Russian garrison in Laihia (near Vaasa) ended in untrained White Guards there panicking, with some...

cards.title: Jaeger Return to Finland
cards.it: The card image shows a contingent of jaeger being received by the commander-in-chief Mannerheim, in the marketplace in the town of Vaasa. See also #10 above.

cards.title: Reds Major Offensive
cards.it: In February 1918, the Reds launched a major offensive on all fronts. A harbinger of the Reds military ineptitude, it failed to produce any notable results. The next offensive was planned and partially executed in March of 1918. By that time, however, Senate forces were already in the midst of an operation to retake Tampere (see #40 Battle of...

cards.title: Hennala
cards.it: This was a former Russian garrison base in the town of Lahti (see Event #41), was the location of the one of the more notorious Senate prison camps. Formed in May 1918, at the end of the war, it housed over 20,000 Red prisoners and refugees. The camp—essentially an open field—was not equipped to handle such a large number of prisoners. The...

cards.title: War with Many Names
cards.it: Already during the conflict itself, the war came to bear different names, depending on who was speaking about it. The Senate side viewed it as a “war of liberation” for Finland from Russian influence. Others, such as the Finnish novelist Juhani Aho (1918b: 166), described it as a “war between brothers” to emphasize the particularly tragic...

cards.title: Meetings in the Catacombs
cards.it: The “catacombs” was the nickname of the secret meeting place for those working-class Social Democrats who did not join the Red Revolt, among them Väinö Tanner. The card’s image pictures the building in Helsinki, in the catacomb-like basement where the secret meetings were held (Image: Helsinki City Museum, License CC BY 4.0). For decades, the...

cards.title: German Invasion of Hanko
cards.it: With the treaty of Brest-Litovsk, in March 1918, the Russians agreed to give up a host of their European possessions, including Finland. This freed the Germans to assert themselves in the country. On 3 April, the Germans landed in Hanko, about 77 miles (or 125 kilometers) southwest of Helsinki, unopposed. A week later they arrived in Helsinki...

cards.title: Battle of Helsinki
cards.it: The Finnish historian Seppo Hentilä wrote (Jussila et al 1999: 119): The main German force ― the Baltic division, consisting of some 11,000 men under the command of General Rüdiger von der Goltz ― landed in Hankoniemi on 3 April [see Event #31]. Another detachment of some 3,000 men landed in Loviisa on 7 April and invaded Lahti two weeks later...

cards.title: Political Arrests
cards.it: Both the Reds and Whites held suspicions about the true allegiance of the well-known Social Democrat politician Väinö Tanner. Tanner (1949) details a number of failed and successful attempts to arrest him for allegedly supporting the enemy. Tanner survived the war, and in subsequent decades, served in important political roles—through World War...

cards.title: Home Front
cards.it: On 18 February, 1918, the White Senate ordered the conscription of all males aged 21 to 39. By April, an estimated 11,000 conscripts were fighting in the war on the White side. (Haapala & Hoppu 2009: 137) The shaded text on the Event card refers to trains sent by the Finnish Reds to Russia to fetch grain for the purpose of relieving food-supply...

cards.title: Prisoners
cards.it: See Event #28.

cards.title: VATO
cards.it: In the course of 1918, a special purpose department of the Senate forces’ headquarters, named VATO (Valloitettujen Alueiden Turvaamisosasto) or the Department for the Pacification of Conquered Areas, was formed to oversee the management of the prison camps, as well as for other reasons. For instance, the department also directed units in the...

cards.title: Tanner Abroad
cards.it: In the Summer of 1918, after the hostilities had already ended and the White retributions against the Reds were in full swing, the leading Social Democratic politician Väinö Tanner left on a trip to neighboring Sweden. His intention was to inform the Swedish and international media about the White retributions taking place in Finland. Armed...

cards.title: First Post-War Parliament
cards.it: The new Finnish parliament met for the first time on 15 May, 1918. It was a rump parliament of the victor, lacking many of its members, over half of which had been Social Democrats, implicated or killed in the revolt, or escaped to Russia: The Eduskunta [the Finnish parliament] assembled for the first time on 15 May 1918, the day before the...

cards.title: Battle of Tampere
cards.it: One of the fiercest and strategically most important battles of the war, winning the the Battle of Tampere was also a major morale-boost victory for the Senate forces. The order “shoot where you see fit,” referenced in the card’s text, was given by a Red commander (Haapala & Hoppu 2009: 195) indicating the level of poor military organization...

cards.title: Battle of Lahti
cards.it: The town of Lahti lies 62 miles or 100 kilometers north of Helsinki. After the German contingent led by Goltz had taken Helsinki, they headed north towards Lahti, as did the Brandestein contingent from Loviisa. The Germans were quick to defeat the Reds along the way, but not always without taking casualties. On the 20 April, the Senate army and...

cards.title: Battle of Viipuri
cards.it: Having taken Tampere (see Event #33) and secured a strategically important railway junction toward the east at Haapamäki North of Tampere, Mannerheim quickly shifted the emphasis to the eastern front (Mannerheim 1951: 325). Senate forces would soon cut the Reds’ resupply and escape routes to Russia. The move culminated in the capture of the...

cards.title: Rough Justice
cards.it: Terror was an inseparable part of how both the Reds and Senate forces conducted the war. It took increasingly arbitrary forms as the conflict progressed. The Red Revolt, from January 1918 onward, had seen the Red Guards avenge personal retributions on the bourgeoisie and nobility for perceived past injustices. Upon their reconquest of the...

cards.title: Mannerheim's Victory Parade
cards.it: The card’s image shows one of the most memorable photos taken during the war: the commander-in-chief of the White army, Mannerheim, and his entourage, leading the Helsinki victory parade on horseback. The parade was politically charged. As recounted in his memoirs, already on 16 January 1918, Mannerheim had received the promise from the head of...

cards.title: Fate in the Balance
cards.it: This card represents the effects of two episodes, the historical ends of which lie outside the temporal scope of this game, yet they crucially affect some of the processes depicted in the game. © 2023 GMT Games, LLC

cards.title: Propaganda — 3rd
cards.it: This card features a cartoon drawing of a crowd of obviously frightened Red Guards looking at the ominous shadow of a German soldier’s helmet rising on the snow.
